Drais had stumbled on the fundamental insight of the entire bicycle project — that balance is not a property of the machine but a dynamic negotiation between machine and rider — and he had

done it without any theory to guide him. Every bicycle since has been an elaboration of that discovery.

Why the delay? Partly because the miss

obby-horse around 1839, though the evidence is thin and largely retrospective. The claim that stuck belongs to Pierre Micha

ub. Pierre Lallement, who worked in the Michaux orbit before emigrating, took out

The
Michaux *vélocipède* was a genuine commercial phenomenon. By 1868 the workshop was turning out h
undreds; velocipede riding schools opened in Paris, London, and New York; and the first bicycle race was held at the Par
c de Saint-Cloud in May 1868, won by the expatriate Englishman James Moore. The machines were iron-framed with wooden w

heels and iron tyres, and the ride quality over cobbles earned them the affectionate name *boneshaker*.

ive imposed a brutal constraint. One turn of the pedals equalled one turn of the wheel, so top speed was set by wheel circumference and how fast a
human could spin their legs. A 36-inch wheel at 60 rpm gives about 10 mph. To go faster, you enlarged the wheel.

## The Ordinary

Hence the high-wheeler — the penny-farthing, though contemporaries called it the *ordinary*.
James Starley of Coventry, working through the early 1870s, refined it into something remarkable. His
Ariel of 1870 introduced a wheel tensioned by radial wire spokes, and he later developed tangent
spoking, in which the spokes leave the hub at an angle and transmit drive torque in tension rather than tr
ying to resist it in bending. Tangentially spoked wheels are still the standard on every driven bicycle wheel today; the geometry has not been improved up

on in a century and a half.

With wire spokes, a wheel could be five feet across and still light. Solid rubber tyres took the worst ed
ge off the roads, hollow steel tubing cut frame weight, and ball bearings — patented for
bicycle use in this period — reduced friction dramatically. The ordinary was a machine of real performance: fast, efficient, and genuinely th

rilling.

It was also lethal. The rider sat almost directly above the front hub, five feet up, with their centre of mass ahead of and above the contact pat

the ground. The manoeuvre was known as *taking a header*, and it killed people. Mounting required a running start and a step pe
g; dismounting at speed was an art. High-wheeling was, in practice, a sport for athletic young men,

and the machine's entire social reach was limited by that fact.

Attempts at safer designs proliferated.
Tricycles found a market among women, whose clothing made the ordinary impossible, and among older and more cautious riders — James Starley's Sal
vo tricycle of 1877 gave the world the differential gear, which passed from bicycles into the automobile and remains in every car on the
road. Various dwarf ordinaries and geared designs tried to shrink the front wheel while preserving the ratio. But the real

answer was to give up on driving the front wheel at all.

The chain drive was the hinge on which the whole history turns. A ch
ain running from a pedal-driven sprocket to a smaller sprocket on the rear wheel decouples gearing from wheel size entirely.
Choose the sprocket ratio and you choose the gear; the wheels can then be sized for ride quality and handling rather than for speed. Both wheels can

Rover Safety Bicycle had two wheels of similar moderate size, a rear chain drive, direct steering to the front wheel, and a diamond-ish frame.

structure that carries rider load and pedalling torque almost entirely in tension and compression rather than bending. It is a super

entially the same thing in 1847, a fact that later invalidated Dunlop's patent. Air-filled tyres transformed everything. They c

beat racers on solids so decisively that the market converted almost overnight.

modern bicycle existed: diamond frame, chain drive to the rear wheel, tangent-spoked wheels of equal size, ball bearings, pneumatic tyres. The

remaining century of development would refine materials and add gears, but the architecture was fixed.

om and Its Consequences

What followed was one of the great consumer manias of the nineteenth century. Between roughly 1890 and 1897, bicycle production ex
ploded across Britain, France, Germany, and the United States. Prices fell from luxury to attainable. Millions of people acquired, for the first time in

human history, cheap personal mechanised mobility.

The social effects were immediate and radical. The bicycle broke the ge
ographic limits of courtship and marriage in rural districts. It gave working people access to countryside and coast
. And it collided head-on with the constraints on women's dress and movement, in ways that made it a gen
uine political object. Susan B. Anthony's remark in 1896 is quoted so often that it has gone slightly lim
p, but she meant it plainly: the bicycle had done more for the emancipation of women than anything else. Rational dress — bloomers, divided skirts — advanced on the back
of the bicycle because riding in the prevailing costume was impossible. Cycling clubs became the first mass mix
ed-sex leisure organisations in many countries. The Good Roads Movement in America, agitating for paved surfaces, was a cyclists

' campaign; it paved the way, quite literally, for the motorcar that would displace them.

The industrial leg
acy was equally large. Bicycle manufacture taught precision metalworking, ball bearings, chain drive, tubular frames, and differ
ential gears to a generation of engineers who moved straight into motorcycles, cars, and aircraft. The Wright brothers were bicycle mechanics. So were Morris, Rover, Opel, Pe

ugeot, and Škoda. The bicycle was the apprenticeship of the twentieth-century vehicle industry.

## The Problem of Gears

One thing the
safety bicycle could not do was change ratio. A chain gives one gear, and one gear is a compromise between the flat and the hill.

Solving this took another sixty years of ingenuity.

The first workable approaches avoided moving the chain. Riders used flip-flop
hubs, with a sprocket on each side of the rear wheel: stop, remove the wheel, turn it around, reinstall. Better
was the internally geared hub — the Sturmey-Archer three-speed, patented in 1902, used epicyclic gearing inside the
hub shell to give direct drive plus a step up and a step down. It was sealed, robust, shiftable at a standstill, and it d

ominated everyday cycling in Britain and northern Europe for most of the century. Its limitation was weight and a narrow ratio range.

The derailleur — from
the French *dérailler*, to derail — took a different approach: move the chain sideways from one sprocket to another while it is running. Paul de V
ivie, the French cycling evangelist who wrote under the name Vélocio, was experimenting with multi-speed sh
ifting systems in the 1900s and campaigning for them relentlessly. Early designs from Le Cyclo and others in the 1920s and
1930s put two to four sprockets on the rear hub, moved by a rod-and-lever mechanism, often requ

iring the rider to back-pedal and to adjust chain tension separately.

The organisational obstacle was as large as the technical one. Henri Des
grange, who ran the Tour de France, regarded gears as a form of cheating — an affront to the moral seriousness of suffering — and ban
ned derailleurs from the race until 1937. Riders had used the flip-flop hub instead, dismounting on climbs to reverse their w

heels.

The design that resolved the problem came from Tullio Campagnolo. A racer himself, he had l
ost a race in 1927 on the Croce d'Aune pass, hands too frozen to loosen his
wheel nuts to change gear — an episode that produced first the quick-release skewer and later a
lasting obsession with shifting. His Gran Sport derailleur of 1951 established the modern form: a parallelogram lin
kage that moves a jockey-wheel cage laterally across the sprockets, with a spring-loaded t
ensioner arm taking up chain slack, all operated by a cable from a lever on the frame. Every derailleur since is a variation on

that parallelogram.

From there development was incremental and continuous: five, then six, seven, and eventually twelve sprockets at the rear; ramped and profiled te
eth to encourage the chain to climb; indexed shifting from Shimano in the 1980s, so a lever click corresponded to exactly one gear; integ

The bicycle did not begin with pedals. It began with a nobleman in Baden pushing himself along a road with his feet.

It was a wooden beam mounted on two in-line wheels of roughly equal size, with a padded rest for the forearms and, crucially, a steerable front wheel. The rider straddled the beam, pushed off the ground, and glided. On his first documented outing Drais covered some fourteen kilometres in under an hour, roughly four times walking pace.

The steering is the part that matters, and it is easy to underrate. A two-wheeled vehicle in line is statically unstable; it stays upright only because the rider continuously steers into the fall. Drais had stumbled on the fundamental insight of the entire bicycle project — that balance is not a property of the machine but a dynamic negotiation between machine and rider — and he had done it without any theory to guide him. Every bicycle since has been an elaboration of that discovery.

The draisine, or hobby-horse or dandy-horse as the English called it, enjoyed a brief and slightly ridiculous vogue. Denis Johnson of London patented an improved version in 1818 and sold it to fashionable young men who raced them on pavements, injured pedestrians, and were promptly banned from several city centres. The machines were heavy, the roads were appalling, and the whole business of propelling oneself by foot on a device that gave no mechanical advantage was — beyond the novelty — simply harder than walking. By the mid-1820s the fad had collapsed. It would be four decades before anyone made the obvious next move.

The social effects were immediate and radical. The bicycle broke the geographic limits of courtship and marriage in rural districts. It gave working people access to countryside and coast. And it collided head-on with the constraints on women's dress and movement, in ways that made it a genuine political object. Susan B. Anthony's remark in 1896 is quoted so often that it has gone slightly limp, but she meant it plainly: the bicycle had done more for the emancipation of women than anything else. Rational dress — bloomers, divided skirts — advanced on the back of the bicycle because riding in the prevailing costume was impossible. Cycling clubs became the first mass mixed-sex leisure organisations in many countries. The Good Roads Movement in America, agitating for paved surfaces, was a cyclists' campaign; it paved the way, quite literally, for the motorcar that would displace them.

The industrial legacy was equally large. Bicycle manufacture taught precision metalworking, ball bearings, chain drive, tubular frames, and differential gears to a generation of engineers who moved straight into motorcycles, cars, and aircraft. The Wright brothers were bicycle mechanics. So were Morris, Rover, Opel, Peugeot, and Škoda. The bicycle was the apprenticeship of the twentieth-century vehicle industry.

## The Problem of Gears

One thing the safety bicycle could not do was change ratio. A chain gives one gear, and one gear is a compromise between the flat and the hill. Solving this took another sixty years of ingenuity.

The first workable approaches avoided moving the chain. Riders used flip-flop hubs, with a sprocket on each side of the rear wheel: stop, remove the wheel, turn it around, reinstall. Better was the internally geared hub — the Sturmey-Archer three-speed, patented in 1902, used epicyclic gearing inside the hub shell to give direct drive plus a step up and a step down. It was sealed, robust, shiftable at a standstill, and it dominated everyday cycling in Britain and northern Europe for most of the century. Its limitation was weight and a narrow ratio range.

The derailleur — from the French *dérailler*, to derail — took a different approach: move the chain sideways from one sprocket to another while it is running. Paul de Vivie, the French cycling evangelist who wrote under the name Vélocio, was experimenting with multi-speed shifting systems in the 1900s and campaigning for them relentlessly. Early designs from Le Cyclo and others in the 1920s and 1930s put two to four sprockets on the rear hub, moved by a rod-and-lever mechanism, often requiring the rider to back-pedal and to adjust chain tension separately.

The organisational obstacle was as large as the technical one. Henri Desgrange, who ran the Tour de France, regarded gears as a form of cheating — an affront to the moral seriousness of suffering — and banned derailleurs from the race until 1937. Riders had used the flip-flop hub instead, dismounting on climbs to reverse their wheels.

The design that resolved the problem came from Tullio Campagnolo. A racer himself, he had lost a race in 1927 on the Croce d'Aune pass, hands too frozen to loosen his wheel nuts to change gear — an episode that produced first the quick-release skewer and later a lasting obsession with shifting. His Gran Sport derailleur of 1951 established the modern form: a parallelogram linkage that moves a jockey-wheel cage laterally across the sprockets, with a spring-loaded tensioner arm taking up chain slack, all operated by a cable from a lever on the frame. Every derailleur since is a variation on that parallelogram.

From there development was incremental and continuous: five, then six, seven, and eventually twelve sprockets at the rear; ramped and profiled teeth to encourage the chain to climb; indexed shifting from Shimano in the 1980s, so a lever click corresponded to exactly one gear; integrated brake-shift levers; and eventually electronic shifting, in which a handlebar button sends a signal to a servo motor.

## The Shape That Stayed

What is striking, looking back across two centuries, is how early the architecture froze. A rider from 1890 set on a modern road bike would find the frame geometry familiar, the chain drive familiar, the wheels familiar. Carbon fibre has replaced steel, tyres have got better, and there are twelve gears instead of one — but the machine is recognisably the same answer to the same problem.

That durability is the real measure of what Drais, the Starleys, Dunlop, and Campagnolo achieved. The bicycle remains the most energetically efficient means of transport ever devised, converting human effort into distance better than walking, running, or any powered vehicle per unit of energy. It was invented before the theory of its own stability was understood, refined by blacksmiths and carriage-makers rather than physicists, and it turned out to be very close to optimal. Two wheels, a triangulated frame, and a chain. It is hard to improve on.
